title: The Seven Virtues
summary: Rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, and pride.

lessons.title: Name the seven
lessons.objective: Name the seven virtues in the unit’s order and keep them as one code.

exercises.prompt: How many virtues does this unit teach?

feedback.note: The unit names seven virtues, from rationality through pride.

exercises.prompt: Match each opening virtue to the job this unit gives it.

pairs.left: Rationality
pairs.right: Use reason to know and to choose

pairs.left: Independence
Integrity
pairs.right: Act on the judgments you accept

feedback.note: The list starts with thinking, then with owning that thought, then with acting on it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two ends of the list.

feedback.note: Rationality is first in the unit summary. Pride is last.

exercises.prompt: After rationality and independence, put the next three virtues in the unit’s order.

feedback.note: The middle of the list is integrity, honesty, then justice. Humility is not one of the seven.

exercises.prompt: Which name is not one of the seven virtues?

feedback.note: Honesty, justice, and pride are on the list. Humility is not.

exercises.prompt: Which pair closes the list?

feedback.note: After justice, the unit names productiveness and then pride.

exercises.prompt: Match the last four virtues to the short job of each.

pairs.left: Honesty
Justice
pairs.right: Judge people by what they do

pairs.left: Productiveness
Pride
pairs.right: Earn the right to respect yourself

feedback.note: These four finish the code: truthfulness, fair judgment, productive work, and moral ambition.

exercises.prompt: Build the full list in the unit’s order.

feedback.note: Keep that order: rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, pride.

lessons.title: Rationality first
lessons.objective: Treat rationality as the virtue of using reason to know the facts and to choose.

exercises.prompt: Which virtue is the use of reason as your way of knowing and choosing?

feedback.note: Rationality is the virtue of guiding both knowledge and action by reason.

exercises.prompt: Match each habit to whether it is rationality.

pairs.left: Look at the facts before you act
Let a wish stand in for a fact
Treat a feeling as proof

feedback.note: A feeling can report your estimate. It does not replace looking at what is.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two steps rationality requires.

feedback.note: Rationality is not thought with no decision, and not a decision with no thought.

exercises.prompt: Build the study line for what reason guides.

feedback.note: Under rationality, reason is the guide for what you know and for what you do.

exercises.prompt: A rational person treats reality as something to do what with?

choices.text: Identify, then act on what is identified
Settle by a show of hands
Set aside when it is inconvenient

feedback.note: Rationality starts from the facts. It does not ask the facts to move out of the way.

exercises.prompt: Why does this unit list rationality before the other six?

choices.text: The others are ways of acting by reason
The names happen to be alphabetical
It is the easiest one to skip
It only matters in a crowd

feedback.note: Independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, and pride each assume you are using your mind.

exercises.prompt: Match each breach to the rational habit it drops.

pairs.left: Refusing to see a known fact
Letting a feeling set the standard
Acting with no check on the conclusion

feedback.note: Rationality means you look, you judge, and you are willing to recheck.

exercises.prompt: Name the virtue that the other six depend on.

parts.text: The basic virtue in this set is

feedback.note: Without rationality, the rest of the list has no method.

exercises.prompt: Which policy is rationality in daily choices?

choices.text: Think as far as the choice requires, then act
Think only when nothing is at stake
Hand every decision to someone else

feedback.note: Rationality is a standing policy of using your mind, not a special occasion.

lessons.title: Independence and integrity
lessons.objective: Separate thinking for yourself from acting on the judgment you have reached.

exercises.prompt: Independence, in this unit, is mainly about what?

choices.text: Taking responsibility for your own judgments
Living with no contact with other people

feedback.note: Independence is the work of your own mind. It is not isolation and it is not stubbornness.

exercises.prompt: Integrity, in this unit, is mainly about what?

choices.text: Acting on the convictions you accept
Keeping your real view secret while you do the opposite
Matching your mood of the hour

feedback.note: Integrity is loyalty in action to the judgment you have already reached.

exercises.prompt: Match each virtue to its focus.

pairs.left: Independence
Integrity
pairs.right: Whether your action matches that judgment

pairs.left: A borrowed script you never checked

feedback.note: One virtue asks who thought it. The other asks whether you live it.

exercises.prompt: Fill the contrast.

feedback.note: You can tell the two apart by that split: judgment, then action.

exercises.prompt: Build the order these two virtues require.

feedback.note: Independence comes in the forming. Integrity comes in the acting.

exercises.prompt: You repeat a conclusion you do not understand because the group likes it. Which virtue fails first?

feedback.note: The judgment is not yours. That is a failure of independence, even before you act.

exercises.prompt: You know the right course and do the opposite to avoid trouble. Which virtue fails?

choices.text: None, if the trouble is real

feedback.note: The judgment is already yours. Dropping it in action is a breach of integrity.

exercises.prompt: Match the case to the virtue it practices.

pairs.left: You check a claim before you accept it
You do what you have judged to be right
You think it through and then live it

feedback.note: The two virtues can be split in a case, and they can stand together.

exercises.prompt: Name each virtue in the sentence.

feedback.note: Keep the names on those two jobs and do not swap them.

lessons.title: Honesty and justice
lessons.objective: Contrast refusing to fake reality with judging people by the facts of what they do.

exercises.prompt: Honesty, in this unit, is the refusal to do what?

choices.text: Fake reality to gain a value

feedback.note: Honesty is not a ban on error. It is the policy of not pretending the facts are something else.

exercises.prompt: Justice, in this unit, means what?

choices.text: Judge people by the facts and treat them as they deserve
Give everyone the same praise no matter what they do
Reward whoever you happen to like
Refuse to judge other people at all

feedback.note: Justice uses the facts about a person, then grants what those facts earn.

exercises.prompt: Match each virtue to its subject.

pairs.left: Honesty
Justice
Pretending, whether about a fact or a person

feedback.note: Honesty faces reality. Justice faces people in the light of reality.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two definitions in study language.

parts.text: reality. Justice gives each person what the facts say they

feedback.note: One verb is about reality: do not fake it. The other is about people: give what is deserved.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that keeps the two virtues distinct.

feedback.note: Honesty stops at what is so. Justice goes on to what that fact means a person should receive.

exercises.prompt: You praise someone for a virtue they did not practice. Which virtue fails?

choices.text: None, if the praise is kind

feedback.note: Praise that the facts do not support is unjust. Kindness is not a substitute for justice.

exercises.prompt: You gain a benefit by pretending a fact is other than it is. Which virtue fails?

choices.text: Pride only, and only if you feel bad later
Productiveness, because any gain counts as work

feedback.note: A value gained by faking reality is a breach of honesty, whether or not a bystander notices.

exercises.prompt: Match the act to the breach or the practice.

pairs.left: Fake a fact to get a value
Reward what was not earned
Name the fact and what it deserves

feedback.note: Faking is the honesty failure. Misplaced reward is the justice failure. Naming both is the practice.

exercises.prompt: An honest mistake differs from dishonesty because you did what?

choices.text: Tried to see the fact and were wrong
Knew the fact and hid it
Nothing different; every error is a lie

feedback.note: Honesty is the policy toward reality. A real effort that misses is not the same as a fake.

lessons.title: Productiveness and pride
lessons.objective: Connect making values with the moral ambition to be worthy of your own life.

exercises.prompt: Productiveness, in this unit, is which policy?

choices.text: Create the values your life needs
Take what other people have made
Wish harder until the work is done

feedback.note: Productiveness is the virtue of making values by thought and effort.

exercises.prompt: Pride, in this unit, means what?

choices.text: Moral ambition: earn the right to respect yourself
Vanity: demand that others admire you

feedback.note: Pride here is earned self-respect, not a claim on an audience.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to the virtue or the opposite.

pairs.left: Make the values you need
Become worthy of the life you are making
Live off values you did not earn

feedback.note: Productiveness supplies values. Pride is the character that has earned them. Taking is neither.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two names.

parts.text: The virtue of making values is
. The virtue of moral ambition is

feedback.note: Keep productiveness on the work and pride on the earned character.

exercises.prompt: Build the link between the two virtues.

feedback.note: Productiveness is the making. Pride is the self-respect that making, and the rest of the code, can earn.

exercises.prompt: Which is pride, rather than vanity?

choices.text: Building a character you can honestly respect
Declaring that no standard applies to you

feedback.note: Pride looks at whether you have earned your own respect. Vanity looks at an audience.

exercises.prompt: A productive person adjusts what?

choices.text: The world, by thought and effort, toward human needs
The facts, so work is unnecessary
Other people, so they must provide

feedback.note: Productiveness reshapes materials and plans. It does not pretend the facts will do the work.

exercises.prompt: Match the result to the virtue that aims at it.

pairs.left: Values brought into existence by work
A self you have made worth esteeming
A wish with no effort and no standard

feedback.note: Work without a moral standard is not yet pride. Self-regard without making or earning is not productiveness.

exercises.prompt: Close the unit’s list.

feedback.note: The seven end where they began in purpose: a mind that produces and a person who can look at that life with earned pride.

exercises.prompt: Which set is the whole code this unit teaches?

choices.text: Rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, and pride

feedback.note: Productiveness and pride finish the list. They do not replace the five virtues that come before them.
